blocks.title: 1. The Core Concept: What Is an Angle?
blocks.content: An angle is simply the measure of a **turn** or **rotation** between two lines that meet at a point. Think of opening a book: the wider you open it, the bigger the angle. Angles are measured in **degrees**, where a full circle is 360 degrees. Understanding angles is the gateway to geometry, trigonometry, and even architecture.

blocks.title: 2. The Rules: The Angle Family
blocks.content:
Memorize these angle types:

• **Acute:** Less than 90 degrees (sharp and small, like a pizza slice).
• **Right Angle:** Exactly 90 degrees (a perfect L-shape, marked with a tiny square).
• **Obtuse:** Between 90 and 180 degrees (wide and lazy).
• **Straight:** Exactly 180 degrees (a flat line).
• **Reflex:** Between 180 and 360 degrees (more than a half turn).

blocks.title: 3. Step-by-Step: Angles on Lines and at Points
blocks.content:
Two critical rules you must never forget:

1. **Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees.** If one angle is 110, the other is 180 - 110 = 70.
2. **Angles around a point add up to 360 degrees.** If three angles at a point are 90, 120, and 80, the missing one is 360 - 290 = 70.
3. **Vertically opposite angles are always equal.** When two lines cross, the angles across from each other are identical twins.

blocks.title: 4. Worked Example: Find the Missing Angle
blocks.content:
Two angles sit on a straight line. One angle is 135 degrees. Find the other.

**Step 1:** Angles on a straight line = 180 degrees.
**Step 2:** Missing angle = 180 - 135 = 45 degrees.

**Final Answer: 45 degrees.**

blocks.title: 5. Common Pitfalls
blocks.content: The most common mistake is confusing 'angles on a straight line' (180) with 'angles around a point' (360). Read the question carefully: does it say the angles are on a LINE or at a POINT? Using 360 when you should use 180 (or vice versa) will give you a completely wrong answer every single time.
